content: Alkali metals, which include lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium, and francium, are highly reactive elements found in Group 1 of the periodic table. Although hydrogen is nominally part of Group 1, it rarely exhibits behavior similar to alkali metals and is not considered one of them. Instead, hydrogen naturally exists as a diatomic gas and requires significantly more energy to remove its single electron compared to alkali metals. The alkali metals are characterized by their highly reactive nature, which makes them rarely found in their elemental form in nature. In laboratory settings, they are typically stored under mineral oil to prevent reactions with air or moisture. These metals tarnish easily, have low melting points, and possess low densities. Potassium and rubidium exhibit weak radioactivity due to the presence of long-lived radioactive isotopes, though this radioactivity is harmless. These metals are soft, silver-colored (with cesium having a golden hue), and have low densities. They react readily with halogens to form ionic salts and with water to produce strongly alkaline hydroxides and hydrogen gas. The general reaction with water can be represented as: Alkali metal + water → Alkali metal hydroxide + hydrogen gas. For example, potassium reacts with water to form potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. These reactions become increasingly vigorous as one moves down the group in the periodic table. Alkali metals have a single electron in their outermost shell, which they readily lose to achieve a stable noble gas electron configuration, forming singly charged positive ions (cations). This property gives them the lowest ionization potentials in their respective periods. However, their second ionization potentials are extremely high, as removing an electron from a noble gas configuration is energetically unfavorable. When dissolved in liquid ammonia, alkali metals form blue paramagnetic solutions due to the presence of free electrons. As the solution approaches saturation, it turns deep purple and eventually metallic. These solutions are excellent reducing agents and good electrical conductors. They are sometimes used as substitutes for the metals themselves because they are easier to handle. However, these solutions are not stable over long periods and eventually react to form the corresponding amides. The alkali metals exhibit clear trends as one moves down the group. Electronegativity decreases, reactivity increases, and melting and boiling points decrease. Density generally increases, with the notable exception of potassium, which is less dense than sodium. Francium, being extremely rare and unstable, has not been studied as extensively as the other alkali metals, but it is assumed to have similar chemistry to cesium. Biologically, sodium and potassium are essential for all known forms of life. They are critical for cellular processes and are found in the cytoplasm of living cells. Sodium chloride (table salt) is a common sodium compound but has been linked to hypertension in humans. A study on elderly adults demonstrated that reducing salt intake modestly can lower blood pressure. Lithium, while not essential for biological functions, has been detected in trace amounts in umbilical cord blood. It is considered a non-essential trace element but has significant medicinal uses. Lithium is a key component in the treatment of severe depression and other mental disorders, such as bipolar disorder. For example, in one case, lithium was used to stabilize the mental functions of a patient with neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but serious condition caused by antipsychotic drugs. Rubidium is not required for any known biological functions and is considered a toxic trace element in humans. Studies have shown that rubidium biomagnifies in marine food chains, with higher concentrations found in predatory animals compared to their prey. Cesium is not typically found in biological systems, but cesium chloride is sometimes used as a medicinal supplement. However, this compound has been shown to be toxic to human physiology and can cause severe side effects, potentially leading to fatal outcomes if not used carefully. Francium, the rarest of the alkali metals, is primarily of interest in physics due to its instability and exotic nature. Its chemical and physical properties are not well-characterized, and it is not found in biological systems. Its rarity and instability make it difficult and dangerous to study, requiring specialized radiochemistry techniques.
